segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I decided this for myself: not to come to you again in grief.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if I grieve you, then who is there to make me glad except the one who is grieved by me?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I wrote this very thing so that when I came I would not have grief from those who ought to have given me joy, being confident about all of you that my joy is the joy of you all.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I wrote to you out of great distress and anguish of heart, through many tears, not so that you would be grieved, but so that you would know the love I have for you, which is greater than you realize.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if anyone has caused grief, it is not me he has grieved but, in some measure—not to press the point too hard—all of you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This penalty imposed by the majority is sufficient for such a person,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that now, on the contrary, you should rather forgive and comfort him, so that such a person is not swallowed up by excessive grief.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore I urge you to confirm your love for him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this is also why I wrote: to find out whether you would stand the test, whether you are obedient in everything.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Anyone you forgive anything, I forgive too. For indeed what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, has been for your sake in the presence of Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that we are not taken advantage of by Satan, for we are not ignorant of his schemes.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When I came to Troas for the good news of Christ, and though a door had been opened for me in the Lord,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I had no relief in my spirit, because I did not find my brother Titus. Instead I said farewell to them and went on to Macedonia.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumphal procession in Christ and through us reveals the scent of the knowledge of him in every place.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we are Christ's fragrance to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to the one a scent from death to death, to the other a scent from life to life. And who is sufficient for these things?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we are not, like so many, peddling the word of God; but from sincerity, as from God and in the sight of God, we speak in Christ.

notes.note: The Greek noun and its verb occur eight times in verses 1–7 and are rendered 'grief' and 'grieve' throughout so that the repetition can be heard. 'Again' most naturally implies that Paul had already made one distressing visit to Corinth, which Acts does not record. Most scholars place this visit between the writing of 1 Corinthians and this letter.

Paul refers to an earlier letter written 'through many tears' (verse 4). Older interpreters identified it with 1 Corinthians; most scholars today think it was a separate letter, sent after the distressing visit, that has not survived. A minority hold that part of it is preserved in chapters 10–13 of this letter.

notes.phrase: in some measure—not to press the point too hard—all of you
notes.traditional: but in part: that I may not overcharge you all
notes.note: The Greek is compressed and can be punctuated in more than one way. The verb means 'to weigh down, burden'; here it is taken as Paul declining to overstate the case, which is the majority view. Others read it as 'not to be too hard on him', and the older English tradition construed the sentence as 'he has grieved me only in part, so that I may not burden you all'.

Paul does not name the offender or the offence. The traditional view identified him with the man living with his father's wife in 1 Corinthians 5; most scholars now think he was someone who personally wronged or defied Paul during the distressing visit. 'The majority' may imply that a minority dissented, though the phrase can also mean simply the congregation as a body.

The verb was used for formally ratifying a decision, will or agreement. Paul is probably asking for a public act by the congregation that restores the man, matching the formal penalty of verse 6, not merely for warmer private feelings.

Literally 'in the face of Christ'. Most modern interpreters take this to mean 'before Christ, with Christ as witness'. The older rendering 'in the person of Christ', meaning as Christ's representative, is possible but less likely by the usage of the period.

The Greek word meant an announcement of good news, such as a victory or a ruler's accession, and a first-century reader heard it that way. 'Gospel' is the traditional English equivalent but now suggests a religious genre or a book. Several modern translations also use 'good news'. The phrase 'for the good news' here means 'to proclaim it'.

The verb refers to the Roman triumph, the parade in which a victorious general displayed his captives and spoils through the city. With a personal object it normally means to lead someone as a captive in that parade, so Paul is most likely picturing himself as God's conquered prisoner on display. The older rendering 'causes us to triumph' lacks support in period usage; some scholars soften the image to 'makes a public display of us'.

Two words are distinguished here: 'scent' (a smell of any kind) in verses 14 and 16, and 'fragrance' (a pleasant smell) in this verse. Together they form the Septuagint's standard phrase for a sacrifice whose smell pleases God. Many scholars also see an allusion to incense burned along the route of a triumphal procession, though this is uncertain.

The verb comes from the word for a small retailer or tavern-keeper, a trade with a reputation for watering the wine and cheating on measures. It was a stock insult aimed at teachers who sold philosophy for profit. It thus carries both ideas: trading in the message for gain and adulterating it in the process.

candidates.reason: Occurs throughout the New Testament and translators split between 'gospel' and 'good news'; readers would be confused by variation from chapter to chapter.
Very frequent, with senses ranging over comfort, encourage, urge and appeal; the sense boundaries and the English for each need fixing, especially across 2 Corinthians 1–7.
The noun and its verb λυπέω are a running theme in 2 Corinthians 2 and 7 and are variously rendered grief, sorrow, pain; one choice is needed to keep the thread visible.
Common across the letters, Gospels and Revelation and rendered variously as affliction, tribulation, trouble, distress, suffering.
The question 'who is sufficient?' in 2:16 is answered by wordplay on the same root in 3:5–6, so the rendering must match across chapters (sufficient, competent or adequate).
